prompt: Match each piece of boxoffice data to the source it came from.
hint: Four sources in section 02.

pairs.right: Made by hand for a case

pairs.left: Last season's real orders, made safe

prompt: Why is every address this course signs up at example.org?
hint: Who could receive a message sent there?

choices.text: Boxoffice accepts no other domain
choices.why: Its rule is only an @ with a dot after it; any domain passes.

choices.text: Reserved: no customer is there
choices.why: Right: it is reserved for examples, and a test message there reaches no stranger.

choices.text: It is the Vila theatre's own domain
choices.why: Nothing says so; the point is that it belongs to no real customer.

choices.text: Accounts there are confirmed without an e-mail
choices.why: Every account gets the same confirmation e-mail; the outbox held five.

prompt: A case says "pay order 1001". On a shared test environment that is never restarted, it passed on Monday and fails on Tuesday, and nobody changed the product. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: What did Monday's run leave behind?

choices.text: The product regressed overnight
choices.why: Nobody changed it; a regression needs a change.

choices.text: The case is too vague for anyone to run it a second time
choices.why: It names an order and an action; the problem is the order's state.

choices.text: Monday's run paid 1001, and it cannot be paid twice
choices.why: Right: consumable data, used up by the run before.

choices.text: Order numbers start again from 1001 every day
choices.why: They start from 1001 after a restart, and this environment is never restarted.

prompt: Section 02 asks that test data be known before a case runs. What does that buy when the case fails?
hint: Two possible culprits.

choices.text: A wrong product is told apart from wrong data
choices.why: Right: only known data answers which of the two it was.

choices.text: The case stops failing, because the data is right
choices.why: Known data can still expose a real defect; that is the point of the case.

choices.text: Nobody has to write a precondition
choices.why: The precondition is exactly where the case says which data it relies on.

choices.text: It satisfies the LGPD
choices.why: The law is about personal data, not about whether data is known.

prompt: What does random.Random(1) give make_accounts.py?
hint: Run it today and tomorrow.

choices.text: Truly random accounts, different on each run
choices.why: A seeded generator is the opposite: the same sequence each time.

choices.text: A limit of one account per run
choices.why: The 1 is the seed; the count comes from the command line.

choices.text: The same accounts on every run
choices.why: Right: on every run and every machine, variety without surprise.

choices.text: Passwords that cannot be guessed by anyone
choices.why: Anyone with the program and the seed gets the same passwords, which is fine for test data.

prompt: On a freshly started boxoffice, Ana runs python3 make_accounts.py 5 and then, without restarting, python3 make_accounts.py 8. How many accounts does the second run create?
hint: Which addresses does the second run try, and which exist already?

prompt: Why would make_accounts.py not find a defect at a 41-character name?
hint: Who chooses a boundary value?

choices.text: Python cannot build a string of 41 characters
choices.why: It can; this program was simply not written to.

choices.text: Boxoffice ignores names sent by a script
choices.why: It answers a script exactly as it answers a browser.

choices.text: Boundary values are chosen, not generated
choices.why: Right: its names are valid by design, and a technique chooses the boundary.

choices.text: A seeded generator makes the same name every time
choices.why: It makes the same list every time, with different names in it.

prompt: Why do the name lists in make_accounts.py include Débora and Gonçalves?
hint: What has a field that only saw "Test User" never been asked?

choices.text: R2 requires every name to have an accent
choices.why: R2 limits the length to 1 to 40 characters and says nothing about accents.

choices.text: To meet é and ç before customers do
choices.why: Right: Test User never asks the field about é or ç.

choices.text: They are the theatre's real members
choices.why: No real person's data is in the program; the lists are invented.

choices.text: Accented names make the passwords stronger
choices.why: Names and passwords are drawn separately.

prompt: Débora Barbosa and Daniel Bezerra both mask to D***** B******. What has masking lost that a keyed pseudonym keeps?
hint: Can a table still tell them apart?

choices.text: The length of each word
choices.why: The length survives masking; that is what a layout test needs.

choices.text: Uniqueness, so joins break
choices.why: Right: the same person must get the same value, and different people different ones.

choices.text: Its status as personal data
choices.why: A mask that keeps an initial and a length may still identify somebody.

choices.text: The first letter
choices.why: The first letter is exactly what this mask keeps.

prompt: Rui suggests replacing each address with its plain SHA-256 hash, with no key, because "a hash cannot be reversed". What is wrong with that?
hint: Who could compute the same hash?

choices.text: Two different addresses would get the same hash
choices.why: Collisions are not the risk here; recognition is.

choices.text: The orders table would no longer join
choices.why: A plain hash is the same everywhere, so it joins; that is part of the problem.

choices.text: Anyone with likely addresses hashes them and compares
choices.why: Right: the key is what stops anyone else computing the code.

choices.text: A hash is too long to fit in the column
choices.why: Length is a detail; the protection is the point.

prompt: Under the LGPD, is a copy pseudonymised with a keyed hash still personal data?
hint: What can whoever holds the key do?

choices.text: Yes: with the key, each row links back to a person
choices.why: Right: only data that cannot be reversed with reasonable effort leaves the law.

choices.text: No, because nobody reading the copy sees a name
choices.why: Not seeing a name is not the test; being able to link it back is.

choices.text: Only if the passwords were left in
choices.why: The passwords were dropped, and the codes still link back.

choices.text: No, the law covers production systems only
choices.why: The law covers the data wherever it is processed, a test environment included.

prompt: Who holds the key that pseudonymise.py uses?
hint: What happens when the copy and the key meet?

choices.text: The tester, to check rows against production
choices.why: Copy plus key turns the copy back into the original.

choices.text: Nobody: it is written inside the script
choices.why: The script reads it from the environment so that it never travels with the file.

choices.text: The data's owner, never the tester
choices.why: Right: the tester gets the copy and never the key.

choices.text: Everyone on the team, stored beside the test copy
choices.why: Then anybody who can open the copy can undo it.

prompt: A delivery note that says "leave it with Débora at number 12" shows that columns of free ___ can carry personal data nobody thought to mask.
hint: Not a name column, not an address column.

prompt: Why does pseudonymise.py drop the password instead of masking it?
hint: Which test reads it?

choices.text: A masked password would fail R2's length rule
choices.why: Masking keeps the length; the reason is that nothing needs it.

choices.text: No test needs it, so it does not travel
choices.why: Right: take only the columns a test needs.

choices.text: The keyed hash cannot handle passwords
choices.why: It could hash any text; there is no reason to keep it at all.

choices.text: Passwords are already anonymous
choices.why: A password is part of an account, and some people reuse theirs elsewhere.

prompt: Run a second time without restarting, make_accounts.py prints "There is already an account with that e-mail." five times. What is wrong?
hint: Read R2 again.

choices.text: Boxoffice 1.1 broke the sign-up rule
choices.why: It is enforcing the rule: an address no other account uses.

choices.text: The seed changed between the two runs
choices.why: The seed is the same, which is why the same five addresses were tried.

choices.text: Nothing: the first run's accounts still exist
choices.why: Right: a case that does not control that state tests its own history.

choices.text: accounts.csv was overwritten, so boxoffice lost the accounts
choices.why: Boxoffice never reads the file; the accounts live in its memory.

prompt: Put these steps in order to sign up the same five accounts again from a known state.
hint: Boxoffice resets by restarting.
items: Stop boxoffice with Ctrl-C in its terminal
Start it again with python3 boxoffice.py
Run python3 make_accounts.py 5 in the other terminal
Check that the outbox holds five e-mails
trap: Running the program before the restart hits the accounts that already exist.

prompt: Match each way of getting a database back to a known state to what it costs.
hint: The table in section 05.

pairs.right: Somebody keeps the saved state up to date

pairs.left: Each case makes its own data
pairs.right: Data piles up, and cases depend on what creates it
A case that fails halfway leaves its data behind

right_distractors: Every case needs a copy of production

prompt: Ana and Rui test on the same shared environment, both booking with the member account. Rui's run uses up the last seats Ana's case needs, and her case fails. What is the fix?
hint: Section 05's fixes, applied per person.

choices.text: Rui stops testing until Ana has finished
choices.why: It works once and turns every run into a queue.

choices.text: Accounts of their own, and a known state for cases that need one
choices.why: Right: neither did anything wrong; the data was shared.

choices.text: Ana reports a defect: seats ran out
choices.why: Seats running out is R4 working.

choices.text: Ana edits her case to expect fewer seats
choices.why: Editing a case until it passes hides the data problem.

prompt: Which of these make a copy of production safer to test with? Choose every one that applies.
hint: Section 04 has three methods and two rules.

choices.text: Dropping every column no test needs
choices.why: Right: the password went for that reason.

choices.text: Replacing addresses with a pseudonym whose key stays with the data's owner
choices.why: Right: joins survive and the tester cannot undo it.

choices.text: Reading the free-text columns for names and addresses
choices.why: Right: a delivery note can carry what no other column does.

choices.text: Sending the key along so testers can debug a row
choices.why: Copy plus key is the original again.

choices.text: Hashing each address with no key
choices.why: Anyone with a list of likely addresses can match them.

prompt: Ana needs names of exactly 40 and 41 characters to test R2's limit. Which source of data fits?
hint: Who chooses a boundary?

choices.text: Made by hand for the case
choices.why: Right: the technique chose the values, so the case carries them.

choices.text: Generated by make_accounts.py with a larger count
choices.why: Its names are valid by design and never reach 41.

choices.text: A pseudonymised copy of production
choices.why: Real names of exactly 40 and 41 characters may not exist, and masking keeps lengths anyway.

choices.text: The account boxoffice starts with
choices.why: Bia Souza has a name of nine characters.
